title: Why did my benchmark stop at N=22? A debugging story in nine bugs
summary: Submission for DEV's Summer Bug Smash — Smash Stories track.  There was a file in my repo called...
author: xbill
content: --- title: "Why did my benchmark stop at N=22? A debugging story in nine bugs" published: true series: Bugs tags: bugsmash, debugging, ai, python --- *Submission for [DEV's Summer Bug Smash](https://dev.to/challenges/dev-summer-bug-smash) — Smash Stories track.* There was a file in my repo called `run_benchmark_1_22.py`. Not 1 to 24, which is what the harness was written to do. Not 1 to 26, which is how many Mersenne exponents the agents know. Twenty-two. A chart in the README — `a2a_latency_times_1_22.png` — agreed. At some point, past-me had decided the benchmark ends at 22, committed the evidence, and moved on. This summer, hunting for a Bug Smash target, I finally asked: *why 22?* ## The setup [`a2a-benchmark`](https://github.com/xbill9/a2a-benchmark) compares A2A agent performance across four languages. Python and Go sit behind Gemini tool-calling (ADK); Node and Rust are bare HTTP handlers. Each computes Mersenne primes with Lucas–Lehmer; a harness sweeps N from 1 to 24 and draws two charts. I ran the full sweep. At N=24, the Python column printed `N/A`. Every other language returned data. There it was — not a decision, a **crash**, worked around by shortening the run until it stopped hurting. ![The old chart: the benchmark's world ended at N=22](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/xbill9/a2a-benchmark/bugsmash-assets/docs/bugsmash/before_calc_times.png) ## The 4,300-digit wall The Python agent's response at N=24 wasn't even subtle about it: ```plaintext "Exceeds the limit (4300 digits) for integer string conversion; use sys.set_int_max_str_digits() to increase the limit" ``` CPython 3.11 added a default cap on `int→str` conversion — 4,300 digits — as a denial-of-service mitigation. My agent stringified every prime it found. The 24th Mersenne prime, 2^19937−1, has **6,002 digits**. Here's the part that made me laugh out loud: the stringified list was *never returned*. The tool reports only its elapsed time. The line that had silently amputated my benchmark at N=23 was decorative. The fix was `git rm` energy: delete the `str()`, keep the raw int. Go had the identical dead weight (`val.String()`) inside its timed region — it just happened not to crash. One deleted expression, and a column of data that had never existed came into being: N=24, Python, 2,425.9 ms. ## It gets worse before it gets better With the agents finally running, I kept pulling the thread. The harness parsed Python's elapsed time out of the **LLM's prose** with `r"It took ([\d\.\-e]+) seconds"`. Gemini, in my captures, never once said "It took" — it said *"Calculating the first 5 Mersenne primes took…"* and later *"The calculation took…"*. The only reason the benchmark had Python data at all was a fallback that read the structured tool artifact. My measurement pipeline's primary path was a bet on a language model's phrasing habits. The direct agents had their own tells. Ask Node or Rust for 100 Mersenne primes and they'd cheerfully report `"Found first 100 Mersenne primes"` — having computed 26, the size of their exponent table. And they formatted elapsed time as `%.2f` ms, so Rust's fastest runs reported `0.00ms`, which parses to zero, which cannot exist on a log-scale chart. Those points didn't look wrong; they looked like nothing. And the biggest lie was the chart itself: "A2A Round-Trip Time (including LLM/Tool calling)". Only half true — literally. Two of the four agents route through Gemini; two never touch an LLM. Median RTT: 2.6ms and 4.6ms for the direct pair, ~1.6s and ~1.8s for the Gemini pair. A **~400× gap** presented as a language comparison was actually a pipeline comparison. ## The encores I fixed everything and re-ran the sweep to generate the "after" charts. Go's N=1 datapoint: `N/A`. Cause: my fix. With the dead formatting deleted, Go's small-N runs got so fast that `time.Duration` switched output units — `Elapsed time: 836ns` — and the harness parser had branches for µs, ms, and s, but had never met a nanosecond. **The fix made the code too fast for its own benchmark.** ![After: direct vs Gemini-brokered series, finally labeled as what they are](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/xbill9/a2a-benchmark/bugsmash-assets/docs/bugsmash/after_rtt.png) Parser patched. Re-ran again. Three Go datapoints missing — different ones. The captured response text: > "I already did that. Do you want to do it again?" The harness reused deterministic context IDs; ADK keeps per-context session history; on a rerun, Gemini looked at the old conversation and declined to redo the work. My benchmark's completeness now depended on a language model's opinions about repetition. Unique per-run IDs fixed it, and the final sweep came back **96/96**. ## What I actually learned 1. **The workaround you commit is the bug you keep.** `run_benchmark_1_22.py` sat in the repo like a fossil of an uninvestigated crash. The moment you rename the script instead of reading the stack trace, you've decided to ship the bug. 2. **Benchmarks are production code.** Mine crashed, lied about counts, rounded away its smallest measurements, and compared two different architectures on one axis. Every chart it ever produced was quietly wrong in four ways. 3. **If a machine consumes the output, never route it through prose.** Structured tool artifacts existed the whole time; the regex on LLM text was pure fragility. 4. **An LLM in the measurement path adds failure modes that have nothing to do with the code under test** — including, apparently, boredom. Nine bugs. Four PRs ([#1](https://github.com/xbill9/a2a-benchmark/pull/1), [#2](https://github.com/xbill9/a2a-benchmark/pull/2), [#3](https://github.com/xbill9/a2a-benchmark/pull/3), [#4](https://github.com/xbill9/a2a-benchmark/pull/4)). One question I should have asked a year ago: *why 22?* Don't take my word for any of it — `docker run --rm -e GEMINI_API_KEY=your_key -v "$PWD/out:/out" xbill9/bugsmash` runs all four fixed agents and the full sweep, and writes the charts to `./out`. *Disclosure: I ran this investigation with Claude Code as the debugging agent — it did the reproduction, the fixes, and the benchmark reruns while I steered. The bugs, the numbers, and the "I already did that" refusal are all real and archived in the repo.*

title: 26B Gemma 4 QAT Deployment with GCE g2-standard, NVIDIA L4, MCP, and Antigravity CLI

author: xbill
content: --- title: 26B Gemma 4 QAT Deployment with GCE g2-standard, NVIDIA L4, MCP, and Antigravity CLI published: true series: Gemma4 date: 2026-07-14 14:37:30 UTC tags: gce,mcps,gemma4,googleantigravity canonical_url: https://xbill999.medium.com/26b-gemma-4-qat-deployment-with-gce-g2-standard-nvidia-l4-mcp-and-antigravity-cli-ba89660ae35d --- This article provides a step by step deployment guide for Gemma 4 to a Google Compute Engine hosted GPU enabled system. A suite of Python MCP tools is built to simplify management of the vLLM hosted Gemma 4 deployment with Antigravity CLI. ![](https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1*ljXAWE54fHTvDdCtrPyw1Q.jpeg) #### What is this project trying to Do? This project is a DevOps/SRE assistant that uses a Gemma 4 model hosted on GCE with GPU. It provides tools to provision the Docker container and deploy the model, as well as for observability and performance testing. This project is similar to a previous project that targeted GPU hosted Gemma4 instances on GCP: [Gemma-SRE: Self-Hosted vLLM Infrastructure Agent](https://medium.com/google-cloud/gemma-sre-self-hosted-vllm-infrastructure-agent-afda000c0943) #### Antigravity CLI Antigravity CLI is the follow-on successor to Gemini CLI- the terminal driven, agent assisted coding tool. Full details on installing Antigravity CLI are here: [Getting Started with Antigravity CLI](https://medium.com/google-cloud/getting-started-with-antigravity-cli-26c5da90951f) #### Testing the Antigravity CLI Environment Once you have all the tools in place- you can test the startup of Antigravity CLI. You will need to authenticate with a Google Cloud Project or your Google Account: ```plaintext agy ``` This will start the interface: ![](https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1*lqIZz4wq1OG2KfDHUiEhcQ.png) #### Full Installation Instructions The detailed installation instructions for Antigravity CLI are here: [Getting Started with Antigravity CLI](https://medium.com/google-cloud/getting-started-with-antigravity-cli-26c5da90951f) #### Python MCP Documentation The official GitHub Repo provides samples and documentation for getting started: [GitHub - modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk: The official Python SDK for Model Context Protocol servers and clients](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk) #### Where do I start? The strategy for starting MCP development for model management is a incremental step by step approach. First, the basic development environment is setup with the required system variables, and a working Antigravity CLI configuration. Then, a minimal Python MCP Server is built with stdio transport. This server is validated with Antigravity CLI in the local environment. This setup validates the connection from Antigravity CLI to the local server via MCP. The MCP client (Antigravity CLI) and the Python MCP server both run in the same local environment. #### Setup the Basic Environment At this point you should have a working Python environment and a working Antigravity CLI installation. The next step is to clone the GitHub samples repository with support scripts: ```shell cd ~ git clone https://github.com/xbill9/gemma4-tips ``` Then run **init.sh** from the cloned directory. The script will attempt to determine your shell environment and set the correct variables: ```shell g2-4-26B-qat-L4-devops-agent source init.sh ``` If your session times out or you need to re-authenticate- you can run the **set\_env.sh** script to reset your environment variables: ```shell g2-4-26B-qat-L4-devops-agent source set_env.sh ``` Variables like PROJECT\_ID need to be setup for use in the various build scripts- so the set\_env script can be used to reset the environment if you time-out. #### Model Management Tool with MCP Stdio Transport One of the key features that the standard MCP libraries provide is abstracting various transport methods. The high level MCP tool implementation is the same no matter what low level transport channel/method that the MCP Client uses to connect to a MCP Server. The simplest transport that the SDK supports is the stdio (stdio/stdout) transport — which connects a locally running process. Both the MCP client and MCP Server must be running in the same environment. The connection over stdio will look similar to this: ```python # Initialize FastMCP server mcp = FastMCP("Self-Hosted vLLM DevOps Agent") ``` #### Running the Python Code First- switch the directory with the Python version of the MCP sample code: ```plaintext ~/gemma4-tips/g2-4-26B-qat-L4-devops-agent ``` Run the release version on the local system: ```shell make install Processing ./. ``` The project can also be linted: ```shell xbill@penguin:~/gemma4-tips/g2-4-26B-qat-L4-devops-agent$ make lint ruff check . All checks passed! ruff format --check . 7 files already formatted mypy . Success: no issues found in 7 source files Success: no issues found in 6 source files ``` #### Getting Started with Gemma 4 on GPU The Official vLLM repo also has Gemma4 specific information: [Releases · vllm-project/vllm](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/releases) #### Gemma 26B Gemma 2B is the latest model in the Gemma4 series. More details are available here: [google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it · Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it) and here: [Get started with Gemma models | Google AI for Developers](https://ai.google.dev/gemma/docs/get_started) #### NVIDIA L4 on GCE The NVIDIA L4 support on Google Cloud Compute Engine is documented here: [Introducing G2 VMs with NVIDIA L4 GPUs | Google Cloud Blog](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/compute/introducing-g2-vms-with-nvidia-l4-gpus) #### Quantization-Aware Training (QAT) One of the key issues with deploying models is available GPU memory based in the hardware footprint. Along with the new 2B model release- new versions of the model that use QAT to reduce the memory requirements have been released: [Gemma 4 QAT models: Optimizing model compression for mobile and laptop efficiency](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/developers-tools/quantization-aware-training-gemma-4/) #### QAT Model Versions What are the differences between the versions on Hugging Face? ```markdown > what is the difference between gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-qat-q4_0-unquantized and gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-qat-q4_0-gguf and google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-qat-w4a16-ct While we wait for your 26B model to finish loading its weights into the GPU, here is the breakdown of the differences between those three specific Gemma 4 26B MoE (Mixture of Experts) QAT variants: ### 1. gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-qat-q4_0-unquantized • Format: High-precision weights (usually bfloat16). • What it is: These are the "master" weights that came directly out of the Quantization-Aware Training (QAT) process. Even though they are stored in high precision, the model has already "learned" how to behave like a 4- bit model. • Primary Use: You would use this if you want to convert the model to a new, custom format or for research purposes where you need the full precision gradient/activation data. ### 2. gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-qat-q4_0-gguf • Format: GGUF (GPT-Generated Unified Format). • What it is: This version is quantized using the q4_0 method (4-bit quantization) specifically for the llama.cpp ecosystem. • Primary Use: Local deployment. This is what you would use if you wanted to run this 26B model on your laptop, an Apple Silicon Mac (using LM Studio/Ollama), or a consumer NVIDIA GPU with limited VRAM. It is optimized for "one user" scenarios with low latency. ### 3. google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-qat-w4a16-ct • Format: Compressed-Tensors ( -ct ) with w4a16 (4-bit Weights, 16-bit Activations). • What it is: This is the version we are currently deploying on your GCE instance. It uses the compressed- tensors standard natively supported by vLLM. • Primary Use: Cloud/Enterprise Serving. It is designed for high-concurrency environments (multiple users at once). Because it keeps the activations in 16-bit while quantizing weights to 4-bit, it maintains higher accuracy for complex tasks like tool-calling and reasoning compared to standard 4-bit formats. ────── ### Summary Comparison Table Feature | Unquantized | GGUF ( q4_0 ) | Compressed-Tensors ( w4a16-ct ) -------------------------|-------------------------|------------------------|---------------------------------- Precision | bfloat16 (High) | 4-bit (Compressed) | 4-bit Weight / 16-bit Activation Target Engine | PyTorch / Transformers | llama.cpp / Ollama | vLLM / SGLang Best Hardware | Research Servers | Mac Studio / Local PCs | NVIDIA L4 / A100 / H100 Main Advantage | Maximum Fidelity | Smallest File Size | Highest Throughput │ [!NOTE] │ All three models share the 26B-A4B architecture, which means they have 26 Billion total parameters, but only │ ~4 Billion are active for any single token generation (Mixture of Experts), allowing for the speed of a 4B │ model with the knowledge of a 26B model. ``` More documentation is available here: [Gemma 4 model overview | Google AI for Developers](https://ai.google.dev/gemma/docs/core#qat) #### MCP stdio Transport One of the key features that the MCP protocol provides is abstracting various transport methods. The high level tool MCP implementation is the same no matter what low level transport channel/method that the MCP Client uses to connect to a MCP Server. The simplest transport that the SDK supports is the stdio (stdio/stdout) transport — which connects a locally running process. Both the MCP client and MCP Server must be running in the same environment. In this project Antigravity CLI is used as the MCP client to interact with the Python MCP server code. #### Antigravity CLI mcp\_config.json A sample MCP server file is provided in the .agents directory: ```json { "mcpServers": { "gpu-devops-agent": { "command": "python3", "args": [ "/home/xbill/gemma4-tips/gpu-26B-qat-L4-devops-agent/server.py" ], "env": { "GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT": "aisprint-491218", "GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION": "us-east4", "VLLM_BASE_URL": "https://gpu-26b-qat-l4-devops-agent-289270257791.us-east4.run.app", "MODEL_NAME": "/mnt/models/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-qat-w4a16-ct" } } } } ``` #### Validation with Antigravity CLI The final connection test uses Antigravity CLI as a MCP client with the Python code providing the MCP server: ```plaintext MCP Servers Plugins (~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/plugins) > ✓ google-dev-knowledge Tools: search_documents, answer_query, get_documents ✓ gpu-devops-agent Tools: save_hf_token, get_vllm_endpoint, list_vertex_models, list_bucket_models, analyze_cloud_logging, +26 more ``` #### Model Lifecycle Management via MCP The MCP tools provide a complete suite of agent-oriented operations for managing vLLM deployment on GCE, Cloud Run or a TPU. Overview of MCP tools : ```markdown Here is the output of the get_help tool: ### 🛠️ GCP Gemma 4 SRE Agent Help & Configuration You can configure this MCP server using the following environment variables: GCP Configuration: • GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT : Your GCP Project ID. • Current Value: comglitn • GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION : The GCP Region/Location. • Current Value: us-east4 • GOOGLE_CLOUD_ZONE : The GCP Zone for GCE VM deployment. • Current Value: us-east4-a • BUCKET_NAME : GCS Bucket used to store model weights. • Current Value: comglitn-bucket • MODEL_NAME : Default Hugging Face repository or GCS path. • Current Value: google/gemma-4-2B-it-qat-w4a16-ct • VLLM_BASE_URL : The explicit URL of your vLLM GCE service. (If not set, it is auto-discovered via GCE VM external IP) • Current Value: Not set (auto-discovering) #### 🐳 Infrastructure & Deployment • start_gce : Starts an existing GCE instance, or provisions a new one if none exists. • status_gce : Checks GCE instance status. • stop_gce : Stops GCE instance. • check_vllm : Checks the status of the vLLM container and engine running on the GCE instance. • deploy_vllm : Deploys vLLM to GCP GCE g2-standard-4 (NVIDIA L4) VM instance. • destroy_vllm : Deletes the GCP GCE vLLM VM instance. • status_vllm : Checks GCE instance status. • update_vllm_scaling : Scales GCE instance type vertically. • get_vllm_deployment_config : Generates the gcloud compute command and startup script. • get_vllm_gpu_deployment_config : Generates a GKE manifest for GPU (NVIDIA L4). • check_gpu_quotas : Checks GPU/Accelerator quotas for a region. • get_vllm_endpoint : Returns the current active vLLM endpoint URL. #### 📊 Model Management • list_vertex_models : Lists models in the Vertex AI Registry. • list_bucket_models : Lists model weights in GCS bucket. • save_hf_token : Securely saves a Hugging Face API token to Secret Manager. • get_vertex_ai_model_copy_instructions : Instructions to copy model from Vertex AI Model Garden to GCS. • get_huggingface_model_copy_instructions : Instructions to download model from Hugging Face and upload to GCS. • get_huggingfacehub_download_path : Resolves local cache path using huggingface_hub. #### 📊 Monitoring & Status • get_metrics : Fetches raw Prometheus metrics from the running vLLM service's /metrics endpoint. • get_system_status : Provides a high-level status dashboard of the service and health. • get_endpoint : Verifies connectivity and returns the active service URL. • get_model_details : Retrieves detailed model metadata and engine state from /v1/models . • verify_model_health : Deep health check by querying the model with a simple prompt and measuring latency. #### 📈 Performance & Benchmarking • run_benchmark : Runs performance/concurrency benchmark sweeps against the vLLM GPU endpoint. #### 💬 Interaction & Diagnostics • query_gemma4 : Primary tool to query the self-hosted model with standard chat message format. • query_gemma4_with_stats : Queries the model and returns streaming performance statistics (TTFT, throughput). • query_vllm : Direct text completions querying tool. • analyze_cloud_logging : Fetches logs from GCP Logging and analyzes them using the model. • analyze_gpu_logs : Fetches service logs and uses Gemma 4 to analyze them for SRE/DevOps errors. • suggest_sre_remediation : Suggests remediation plans for SRE errors using the model. ``` #### Find and Exterminate First find a zone with available GPU: ```markdown The find_quota scan across multiple Google Cloud regions is complete. You have significant available quota for NVIDIA L4 GPUs in several regions. ### ✅ Available NVIDIA L4 Quota Summary All listed regions currently show 8 units of available quota (both standard and Spot/Preemptible): • us-central1 (Iowa) • us-east1 (South Carolina) • us-east4 (Northern Virginia) - Note: While quota is available, us-east4-a previously reported a resource stockout. • us-east5 (Columbus, Ohio) • us-west1 (Oregon) • us-west4 (Las Vegas) • northamerica-northeast1 (Montreal) • europe-west1 (Belgium) • europe-west2 (London) • europe-west4 (Netherlands) • asia-southeast1 (Singapore) ### 🚀 Recommendation Since we encountered a stockout in us-east4-a , I recommend attempting your deployment in one of the following high-availability zones: 1. us-central1-a (Iowa) 2. us-east1-b (South Carolina) 3. us-west1-a (Oregon) deploy_with_search() ``` #### Checking System status The status can be checked with an MCP tool: ```markdown > get_system_status 414.2k in | 3.8k out | 3.0k thinking ● Bash(curl -v http://35.243.250.174:8080/health) (ctrl+o to expand) The Gemma 4 26B MoE QAT system is currently healthy and fully operational. While the automated get_system_status tool is reporting "Offline" due to a configuration mismatch in the background MCP server (which is still defaulting to the 4B instance settings), I have verified the 26B deployment directly. ### 🌀 Gemma 4 26B MoE System Status • Instance Name: gpu-26b-qat-l4-devops-agent • Zone: us-east1-b • External IP: 35.243.250.174 • vLLM Health: 🟢 Online (Verified via direct API check) • Model ID: /mnt/models/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-qat-w4a16-ct • Serving Engine: vLLM (Compressed-Tensors w4a16) ### 📊 Performance Summary • TTFT (Time to First Token): 0.536s • Generation Speed: 62.99 tokens/s • KV Cache: FP8 Enabled • VRAM Utilization: ~95% (Optimized for MoE concurrency) │ [!TIP] │ Your previous query ("What is Gemma?") was successful with the new configuration. If you would like to run a │ full benchmark sweep on this 26B model, you can now use the run_benchmark tool or call │ query_gemma4_with_stats for individual prompts. ``` #### Cross Check The Deployed Model Once the model starts locally- the MCP tool allows for model verification: ```markdown > verify_model_health 5.7k in | 438 out | 367 thinking ● gpu-devops-agent/verify_model_health(Verify model health) (ctrl+o to expand) 588.1k in | 6.4k out | 3.0k thinking ● Bash(rm /home/xbill/.gemini/antigravity-cli/brain/341f5c29-5818-4321-a71f-23056ab20e18/scratc...) (ctrl+o to expand) The model health check is successful. I have verified the deep operational health of the Gemma 4 26B MoE QAT model. ### ✅ Model Health Check: PASSED • Model: /mnt/models/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-qat-w4a16-ct • Status: Healthy 🟢 • Verification Response: "Yes, I am working correctly! How can I help you today?" • Inference Latency: 0.47 seconds (Highly optimized for MoE architecture) ### ⚙️ System Metrics • Active IP: 35.243.250.174 (GCE Instance) • Engine: vLLM with CompressedTensors support. • KV Cache: FP8 enabled (Optimized for context window stability). ``` and model details: ```markdown > get_active_models The active model currently served by the vLLM engine is: ### 🧩 Active Models • Model ID: /mnt/models/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-qat-w4a16-ct • Object Type: model • Owned By: vllm • Max Model Length: 32,768 tokens • Created: 2026-07-12 (Unix: 1783891987 ) This model is the Gemma 4 26B MoE QAT variant, utilizing 4-bit weights and 16-bit activations, optimized for high-throughput serving on your NVIDIA L4 GPU. ``` and status: ```markdown > get status ### 🚀 Gemma 4 26B MoE QAT Status • vLLM Engine: 🟢 Active & Healthy (Verified via direct API check) • Model: google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-qat-w4a16-ct • Instance IP: 35.243.250.174 (Port 8080) • Current Latency: 0.47s (Inference) • Current Throughput: ~63 tokens/s ### 🛠 Infrastructure • Compute Instance: gpu-26b-qat-l4-devops-agent (Running) • Zone: us-east1-b • Accelerator: NVIDIA L4 GPU (16GB VRAM) • Quantization: Weights 4-bit / Activations 16-bit (QAT) ``` #### Check the Cloud GCE VM Once Deployed — the model is visible as a standard VM: ![](https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1*YT4CVZ3JemBcrv6hcATSzg.png) #### Review the Model Check the model details: ```markdown > what are the model details The active model is a Gemma 4 26B Mixture of Experts (MoE) variant, specifically optimized for cloud serving on NVIDIA L4 hardware using Quantization-Aware Training (QAT). ### 🧩 Core Model Metadata • Model ID: /mnt/models/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-qat-w4a16-ct • Architecture: Gemma4ForConditionalGeneration (26B total parameters / 4B active per token). • Quantization: w4a16-ct (4-bit Weights / 16-bit Activations). • Context Window: 32,768 tokens (Max Length). • Storage Path: Local GCS FUSE mount at /mnt/models . ### 🚀 Serving Configuration • Engine: vLLM (Optimized for Compressed-Tensors). • KV Cache: FP8 precision (reduces memory usage to allow for larger batch sizes). • Hardware: 1x NVIDIA L4 GPU (16GB VRAM) on GCP GCE. • Performance: ~63 tokens/second with sub-600ms Time-to-First-Token (TTFT). ### ⚖️ Permissions & Capabilities • Sampling: Enabled (Supports temperature , top_p , etc.) • Logprobs: Enabled (Supports detailed token probability analysis) • Reasoning: Supported (Gemma 4 native tool-calling and reasoning chains) ``` and metrics: ```markdown > get_metrics 12.5k in | 900 out | 360 thinking ● Bash(curl -s http://35.243.250.174:8080/metrics | grep "cache") (ctrl+o to expand) The real-time metrics for the Gemma 4 26B MoE QAT deployment (scraped directly from the vLLM Prometheus endpoint at 35.243.250.174 ) are as follows: ### 📈 Current Performance Metrics • Requests Running: 0.0 (Idle) • Requests Waiting: 0.0 (No queue) • Generation Tokens Processed: 790 (Total since last restart) • KV-Cache Usage: 0.0% (Memory is currently clear) • Prompt Tokens Processed: 75 (Total since last restart) ### ⚙️ Engine Configuration Metrics • GPU Memory Utilization: 0.95 (95% VRAM reserved for KV cache) • KV Cache Dtype: fp8 (High-efficiency 8-bit cache enabled) • Total GPU Blocks: 10,656 • Total KV Cache Capacity: 89,326 tokens • Prefix Caching: Enabled (Optimized for repeated prompts) ### 📊 Token Accounting Metric | Value -------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------- Prefill Tokens (Total) | 75 Generation Tokens (Total) | 790 Cache Hits (Total) | 0 Tokens per GPU Block | 16 │ [!NOTE] │ The model is currently idle but fully initialized. The fp8 KV cache configuration allows for a significant │ context window (~89k tokens) even on a single NVIDIA L4 GPU. ``` Once everything is online — you can send queries to the Model: ```markdown > query_gemma4_with_stats what is gemma? 15.5k in | 418 out | 0 thinking ● Bash(rm /home/xbill/.gemini/antigravity-cli/brain/341f5c29-5818-4321-a71f-23056ab20e18/scratc...) (ctrl+o to expand) ### 📊 Performance Stats (Gemma 4 26B MoE QAT) • Model: /mnt/models/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-qat-w4a16-ct • Time to First Token (TTFT): 0.563s • Total Generation Time: 10.828s • Tokens per Second: 63.03 tokens/s • Total Tokens (approx.): 647 ### 💬 Model Response: "What is Gemma?" │ Gemma is a family of lightweight, state-of-the-art open models developed by Google DeepMind. │ │ If Gemini is Google's massive "closed" engine, Gemma is the smaller "open" sibling designed for developers to │ download, customize, and run locally. It inherits the same research and technology used in Gemini, offering │ high-level reasoning and instruction-following in a compact, efficient format. ### ⚙️ Why use Gemma 4 26B MoE? • Efficiency: Uses Mixture of Experts (MoE), meaning it has the knowledge of a 26B model but only activates ~4B parameters per token for speed. • Privacy: Since it runs on your private GCE instance, data never leaves your infrastructure. • Cost: Once deployed, you avoid per-token API fees while maintaining performance comparable to much larger models. │ [!TIP] │ The model is performing at a highly efficient 63 tokens/second. You can continue using │ query_gemma4_with_stats for further prompts. ``` #### Benchmark the Local Model The local model was benchmarked: ```plaintext The benchmark sweep has completed successfully. Here are the compiled results across all combinations of context window sizes and concurrency levels ``` The analysis is reviewed: ```markdown > summarize benchmark results compare and contrast The 2D Grid Benchmark Sweep for the Gemma 4 26B MoE QAT model is complete. The results demonstrate the high efficiency of the Mixture of Experts (MoE) architecture combined with 4-bit QAT and FP8 KV-caching. The model maintained a 100% success rate up to 1024 concurrent users even at the largest context windows. ### 📊 Performance Summary • Peak Throughput: ~81.8 Requests/sec (at 256 concurrent users). • Context Stability: 100% success rate up to 8192 tokens across all concurrency levels. • MoE Advantage: Typical TTFT remains under 600ms, providing the responsiveness of a 4B model with the reasoning power of 26B. • The "Memory Wall": At the extreme edge (2048 users @ 16k context), the success rate dropped to 48% as the system reached the physical VRAM limits of the NVIDIA L4 GPU. ### 📄 Full Report & Artifacts I have generated a detailed performance analysis which you can view here: • Benchmark Report: benchmark_report_26b.md • Performance Chart: benchmark_chart.png • Raw Data: benchmark_sweep_results.csv ``` This is visualized: ![](https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1*rGMHb3Jd-GA1VHZ-ZHi5EQ.png) #### Compare to Other Deployments The GCE deployment was reviewed: ```markdown > summarize gemma4_family_comparison.md The gemma4_family_comparison.md report evaluates the Gemma 4 QAT family (2B, 4B, 12B, 26B MoE) on a single NVIDIA L4 GPU. ### 🚀 Key Takeaways: • The "MoE Miracle": The 26B MoE model is the clear winner for SRE tasks. It provides 26B-level intelligence but operates at 4B-level speeds (activating only ~4B parameters per token). • Surprising Large-Context Performance: At the 16k context window, the 26B MoE is the fastest model in the entire family, outperforming even the 2B and 4B variants in both latency (4.19s) and throughput. • Throughput Scaling: • 2B QAT: The speed leader for simple tasks (~166 Req/s). • 26B MoE QAT: The efficiency leader (~82 Req/s), consistently beating the 12B dense model. • SRE Recommendation: • Use 4B for high-volume, simple automation. • Use 26B MoE for complex reasoning, multi-tool orchestration, and large-log analysis. It offers the best balance of reasoning depth and serving performance. │ [!NOTE] │ The 26B MoE's ability to outperform smaller models at 16k context suggests its architecture is better │ optimized for large KV-cache blocks when paired with fp8 quantization. ``` what about across other deployments? ```markdown ### 📊 Cross-Deployment Summary Your current configuration on GCE is highly optimized and actually outperforms the AWS L4 deployment in throughput for most standard workloads. Metric | GCE (Current L4) | AWS (Legacy L4) | RTX 6000 (Local) ---------------------------|---------------------------|---------------------------|--------------------------- Peak Throughput | 81.8 Req/s | 72.2 Req/s | ~90 Req/s Avg Throughput (1k) | 50.8 Req/s | 26.1 Req/s | ~85 Req/s Latency (1k context) | 1.52s | 2.70s | how does the GCE with GPU pricing compare to cloud run and other deployment options > how does the GCE with GPU pricing compare to cloud run and other deployment options ● Create(/home/xbill/.gemini/antigravity-cli/brain...1-a71f-23056ab20e18/pricing_comparison.md) (ctrl+o to expand) 20.9k in | 1.8k out | 689 thinking The pricing comparison reveals that your current GCP GCE Spot deployment is by far the most cost-effective way to run the Gemma 4 26B MoE model. ### 💵 Cost Summary (NVIDIA L4) Deployment Option | Hourly Rate (Spot) | Hourly Rate (On-Demand) -------------------------------------|------------------------------------|------------------------------------ GCP GCE (Current) | ~$0.16 / hr | ~$0.62 / hr GCP Cloud Run | N/A | ~$0.67 / hr (active) AWS EC2 | ~$0.30 / hr | ~$0.98 / hr ### 💡 Strategic Breakdown • The Spot Advantage: By using Spot VMs on GCE, you are paying ~75% less than you would on AWS and significantly less than a 24/7 Cloud Run instance. • Cloud Run (Serverless): This only becomes cheaper if your model is idle for more than 75% of the day, as it can "scale to zero." However, with the 26B model, "cold starts" (loading the 13GB weights) can take several minutes, which might degrade user experience. • The MoE Value Proposition: Because the 26B MoE model runs on a single L4 GPU (where a dense 26B model would likely require two), you are getting double the intelligence per dollar. ### 📄 Detailed Report For a full breakdown including "Intelligence per Dollar" analysis, see: • Pricing Comparison: pricing_comparison.md At the current Spot rate, running this 26B-class agent 24/7 costs approximately $115/month, which is vastly cheaper than equivalent per-token costs for large closed models. ``` #### Summary The strategy for using MCP for Gemma 4 GPU deployment with Antigravity CLI was validated with a incremental step by step approach. A minimal stdio transport MCP Server was started from Python source code and validated with Antigravity CLI running as a MCP client in the same local environment. This Python server provided all of the management tools to deploy and troubleshoot GCE Model deployments.

title: 5 Trends That Defined AI Engineering at World’s Fair 2026
summary: At this year's AIE World’s Fair, AI engineering entered a new phase: building systems around...
author: Richard MacManus
content: --- title: 5 Trends That Defined AI Engineering at World’s Fair 2026 published: true date: 2026-07-14 23:21:21 UTC tags: canonical_url: https://www.latent.space/p/aiewf26trends cover_image: https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!3Be9!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd4e070d1-3be3-48a9-a86b-ceaf34f4577b_1672x941.png --- #At this year's AIE World’s Fair, AI engineering entered a new phase: building systems around agents, rather than just building with agents. _swyx’s note: thanks to [Richard](http://x.com/ricmac) for covering AIE while I was working on the conference itself! Make sure you have [opted into](https://www.latent.space/account) the [AINews](https://www.latent.space/s/ainews) feed to get our weekday updates. AIE next returns to [NYC, Oct 12-14](https://www.ai.engineer/nyc/2026), with a heavy focus on AI in Finance this year._ * * * AI engineering has come a long way in three years. When swyx[coined the term “AI engineer”](https://www.latent.space/p/ai-engineer) in June 2023, he was giving a name to a new kind of developer emerging from the big bang of large language models. It seems like ancient history now, but remember when we called the intersection of AI and software development “prompt engineering”? That was[just months before](https://ricmac.org/2023/05/12/ai-has-become-integral-to-the-software-delivery-lifecycle/) swyx’s reframing. The latest[AI Engineer World’s Fair](https://www.ai.engineer/worldsfair/2026) showed just how much the field has matured. Whether or not “AI engineer” has become a formal job title everywhere is almost beside the point. The engineering practices that have developed around AI over the past three years — building coding agents, designing harnesses, managing context, evaluating model outputs, and orchestrating increasingly autonomous systems — are **becoming part of mainstream software development**. Rather than focusing on individual announcements at AIEWF, this post will pick out five larger trends that show where AI engineering stands in 2026. ## **1: The focus shifts from agents to the systems around them** One of the clearest ways to see how AI engineering has evolved is to compare two essays by former OpenAI researcher, and now co-founder of Thinking Machines Lab, Lilian Weng. Her influential 2023 article,[LLM Powered Autonomous Agents](https://lilianweng.github.io/posts/2023-06-23-agent/), described the anatomy of an LLM agent in terms of planning, memory and tool use. AutoGPT, BabyAGI and GPT-Engineer were among her examples — proof-of-concept systems that suggested autonomous agents might soon become practical. Her new 2026 essay,[Harness Engineering for Self-Improvement](https://lilianweng.github.io/posts/2026-07-04-harness/), takes a very different perspective. Rather than focusing on the agent itself, Weng argues that the system surrounding the model has become just as important: the harness that manages workflows, context, permissions, evaluation, persistent state and continuous improvement. In other words, AI engineering has moved beyond prompting models toward engineering reliable systems around them. ![Coding agent loop](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!IIql!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd5bc65b2-d2e4-48f5-9e7d-3cd886c70aa5_2048x681.png) Coding agent loop; Image by Lilian Weng   This shift was very much top of mind at AIEWF. I don’t think AutoGPT — the buzzy autonomous agent project [everyone was talking about in 2023](https://ricmac.org/2023/10/13/ai-engineer-summit-wrap-up-and-interview-with-co-founder-swyx/) — was even mentioned this year. Instead, the conversation revolved around Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor, Warp and all the infrastructure needed to make coding agents dependable in production. I remember being turned off by the AutoGPT buzz at the 2023 event, mainly because all the discussions seemed to focus on removing humans from the equation. But over the past few years we’ve learned that **complete agent autonomy is not only unreliable, it isn’t even desirable — especially at scale**. So it was a relief that at AIEWF, agents were largely positioned as augmenting the AI engineer, rather than replacing them. During the OpenAI keynote on day 2 at AIEWF, Romain Huet emphasized this point. Using tools like OpenAI’s Codex, Huet argued, engineers can more easily collaborate with agents. As he put it, “software ate the world, and then AI ate software, but now what we’re here to say is that the AI engineers are eating the world.” {% embed https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pMggiOb18tc %} Despite the growing power of AI engineers, there’s also a sense that even the frontier companies don’t fully understand how their models are evolving — and so how much control can engineers truly have over them? [In a separate keynote](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9fubhllmsBU&t=6s), Anthropic’s [Thariq Shihipar talked about how their latest model, Claude Fable](https://www.latent.space/p/ainews-the-field-guide-to-fable), is like an organic system — **“models are grown, not designed.”** There’s a “capability overhead,” he said, where “Claude gets smarter in a spiky way.” All the more reason to build systems for agentic development, so that we can evaluate and monitor the outputs. ## **2: Loop engineering is the new control layer** By the end of[the first morning of keynotes at AIEWF](https://www.latent.space/p/aiewf-daily-dispatch-loops), it was clear that “loops” was the buzzword du jour of the event. Overuse of the term aside, it did highlight a key point of tension around AI engineering: how much control should agents have, and where should humans remain _in the loop_? ![OpenClaw creator Peter Steinberger advocating for better loops.](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!1tmM!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F3ff8bd9e-2d85-4962-be54-5850906e7fce_1280x851.jpeg) OpenClaw creator Peter Steinberger advocating for better loops.   One approach a lot of leading engineers are now taking is putting themselves in an “outer loop” — to oversee the largely autonomous work being done by agents in an inner loop. **Roland Gavrilescu** is co-founder and CEO of Introspection, a new company building infrastructure for deploying self-improving systems. In[an interview with Latent Space](https://www.latent.space/p/autoresearch-introspection), he explained how the concept of “autoresearch” provides the necessary feedback structure for agent loops: > “_You can think of the system as having an **inner loop** and an **outer loop**. The inner loop is the primary system interacting with users and performing the work. **Autoresearch is more concerned with the outer loop: another system that studies and maintains the primary system**._“ The outer loop can include feedback signals, evals and human input. So it might still be largely autonomous, but the point is it is a method of oversight for the primary agent loop. Former Google engineering leader **Addy Osmani** had a nice line relating to this, saying that “agents can run much more of the inner execution loop, but that outer loop is still engineering.” {% embed https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=n97BCfyFIvw %} The term “loop engineering” came up multiple times during AIEWF, suggesting that it’s the human AI engineer’s responsibility to build these loop systems. Even the “ClawFather” Peter Steinberger, creator of OpenClaw, makes a point of putting himself in the outer loop. In the OpenAI keynote, he explained that **“the agent runs the inner execution loop; I set the direction and I make decisions in the outer loop.”** ![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!SXeX!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2c10ab29-01cc-4c1c-9dd4-1c9937a46fb2_1280x815.jpeg) The Loop Debate at AIEWF.   On the final day, [an on-stage debate was held](https://www.latent.space/p/aiewf-daily-dispatch-locomotives) to determine whether fully autonomous agents were capable of managing loops in reality. **Dex Horthy** from HumanLayer claimed that “the hype is outrunning the discipline.” He wasn’t against loops, per se, noting that Kubernetes is built on control loops — “but they’re deterministic loops.” Geoffrey Huntley, creator of the Ralph Loop, admitted that loops were “frontier thinking,” but he had a wonderful analogy for the audience to ponder: > “_[We’re] kind of like locomotive engineers now. That’s our job: to keep the locomotive on the rails._” {% embed https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c35YoMdnI78 %} ## **3: AI engineering enters the enterprise** This way of working with AI tools is starting to make its way into enterprises, typically via a new role called a “forward deployed engineer” (FDE) — where engineers work directly with organizations to implement AI capabilities. **Natalie Meurer** , who leads FDE at Sierra,[told Latent Space](https://www.latent.space/p/forward-deployed-engineers-aiewf) that implementing AI into organizations typically requires a lot of orchestration. **“Every enterprise we work with wants to know how it can maintain everything its agentic ecosystem is capable of doing,”** she said. “It needs to manage all the integrations and all the teams that contribute to the agent.” ![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!7FmP!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9d9db84e-615f-4389-8e9f-42188bab5b0a_1280x720.jpeg) Cursor’s Pauline Brunet talking about FDEs in an AIEWF session.   In her session at AIEWF, Cursor’s **Pauline Brunet** spoke about what their FDEs look to achieve in each engagement: > _“When [we] walk away at the end of the engagements — and we, in our case, have deployed cloud agents, long-running agents, automations, [and] we’ve built applications on top of our Cursor SDK — that when we walk away, it is a strict ROI for them. **That means they’re not gonna turn things off when we leave.** ”_ Another term used regularly at the conference was “software factory.” At Cursor, “a software factory means long-running agents helping people throughout that entire process,” said Brunet. This is basically what her team of FDEs is responsible for implementing, sitting alongside their customers’ engineers. {% embed https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=APqXGyCoGW4 %} Where human engineers fit into a software factory is a key issue for enterprises. Warp CEO[Zach Lloyd explained](https://www.latent.space/p/software-factories) that organizations need to choose which parts of the lifecycle to automate, and where humans should be brought into the loop. ![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!icur!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8035c7ee-ad6b-4471-be12-cd04aa09231a_1280x800.jpeg) Warp’s Zach Lloyd on building the thing that builds the product.   “You choose your repositories, the parts of the software lifecycle you want to automate, and **the points where humans should be brought into the loop** ,” Lloyd told us, regarding his company’s new software factory platform, Oz. “Different organizations and codebases will have different preferences. Do you fully automate code review? Do you have humans review certain high-risk changes?” Another concern for enterprises is managing their unique organizational data in AI systems. **Prukalpa Sankar** from Atlan spoke at the conference about “context engineering,” explaining in [a tweet](https://x.com/prukalpa/status/2074165485562667177) that it’s important to consider **“​​how context flows from your business systems into a shared company brain, then out to agents** , copilots, and apps through MCP, APIs, and retrieval.” {% embed https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8G_1-3IO4ZQ %} Finally, lest we think enterprises are all-in on agents, Cursor’s [Brunet pointed out](https://www.latent.space/p/cursor-forward-deployed-engineers) that enterprise adoption of AI “is still concentrated among early adopters.” So finding “the right champions inside an organization” is a challenge for FDEs at this stage. ## **4: Coding agents replace IDEs as the developer interface** Perhaps the biggest practical change since the first AI Engineer Summit is how developers interact with AI on a daily basis. In 2023, AI-assisted programming largely meant GitHub Copilot completing the next few lines of code. Most developers were still writing almost everything themselves, using AI as an intelligent autocomplete. **But now we have tools such as Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor and Warp.** These “coding agents” can typically understand a broader objective, explore a codebase, modify multiple files, run tests, debug failures and iterate on their own work before presenting it back to the developer. ![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!uUve!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff4f5e840-6562-422f-9977-5e605e837a99_1280x800.jpeg) In Barr Yaron’s AI engineering survey, coding agents was a key trend.   The trend of coding agents now extends to web development too — with the recent release of Vercel’s eve, which the company calls an “agent framework,” comparable to its popular open source React framework, Next.js. Vercel’s Chief of Software, Andrew Qu,[told Latent Space at AIEWF](https://www.latent.space/p/vercel-agents-new-software) that **agents are effectively a new type of software**. “They [agents] are not as predictable as web applications,” he explained. “The infrastructure can look similar, but the interaction, interface and outputs are much more dynamic.” Qu added that the job of building a framework for agent development is far from over. “A year ago, we did not know sandboxes would become so important, or how much demand there would be for secure code execution and long-running jobs,” he said. “As we learn more from production, there will be much more to build.” ![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!lvum!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F244386b6-1c27-4763-8f5d-af9d239717d4_1280x720.jpeg) A for agents? Andrew Qu flashes the Vercel triangle logo.   This brings us back to the software factory trend, when developers are managing multiple agents. **Charlie Holtz** , CEO of Conductor, reminded the AIEWF audience that regardless of the coding harness, human engineers should always remain in control. “I don’t want the future to be built around factories,” Holtz said. **“I want to feel like a human, I want to be in the flow, I want to be in front of an orchestra, waving my baton.”** {% embed https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=htM02KMNZnk %} There was a sense during the conference that AI engineers aren’t yet aligned on which term is more appropriate: software factories or orchestras? Even Geoffrey Huntley, a loopmaxxing advocate, cautions about getting ahead of ourselves when it comes to automation: > _“My biggest concern is that this time next year at the conference, we’re going to see a whole bunch of folks saying, our factories failed, our loops failed. **These are things that we are still yet to figure out.** ”_ ## **5: Every agent platform is building around skills** One of the talking points of the conference was “skills,” a concept Anthropic popularized when it introduced “agent skills” to Claude[last October](https://claude.com/blog/skills). To borrow [Addy Osmani’s definition](https://github.com/addyosmani/agent-skills), skills “encode the workflows, quality gates, and best practices that senior engineers use when building software.” {% embed https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=n97BCfyFIvw %} At AIEWF, Vercel’s Andrew Qu said that skills were **“useful as portable, on-demand knowledge.”** Introspection co-founder Roland Gavrilescu declared that AI engineering has shifted “from agent tools to agent skills.” {% embed https://x.com/picocreator/status/2071735248472379573 %} In a session on the main stage, **Philipp Schmid** from Google DeepMind showed how using skills (and other declarative Markdown files) allows developers to use “agents without code.” **His main point was that skills reduce the need for orchestration code** , which up till recently was typically done using Python. His conclusion: > “_Agents are just files. We write markdown files to extend capabilities. Agents can learn from those, can create their own files._” {% embed https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0vphxNt4wyk %} **Paul Bakaus** , who used to work for Google but now runs a company called Renaissance Geek, has created an entire project around agent skills. [Impeccable](https://impeccable.style/) is an open source design skills system that gives coding agents a vocabulary for improving interfaces. He even advocates for “skill engineering” as a discipline in its own right. ![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!lpG8!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2c0c711c-6ba9-47b6-b6c3-ba3563ceb862_1280x850.jpeg) Paul Bakaus: “You can’t one-shot design.”   In[an interview with Latent Space](https://www.latent.space/p/skill-engineering-design), **Bakaus argued that most skills — and indeed most models — are not very creative.** “They converge in one direction, and if everybody uses the same skill to do frontend design work or something like that, everything ends up looking the same,” he said. Apparently there’s also such a thing as “skills hell,” which Matt Pocock said is comparable to previous developer frustrations — like frameworks hell. In a virtual presentation, Pocock provided a detailed checklist for writing skills, which you can see in the video below. In a nutshell, **he advises writing fewer and smaller skills, and putting more thought into structure.** {% embed https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UNzCG3lw6O0 %} In a closing keynote, Y Combinator president Garry Tan implored the audience to use skills and other “AI native” approaches at their own startups or employers. Talking about business functions like sales, support and finance, Tan said that “the AI native companies that I see inside YC encode all of that as skills, written procedures that their agents execute, and **they hire engineers whose job it is to maintain those skills, to do the work the skills can’t do yet.** ” {% embed https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eBUyTS7SzV4 %} But again, there’s a danger in relying too much on what agents autonomously do. As AIEWF attendee Tyler Brown [noted on X](https://x.com/tbrownio/status/2073133686288228366), “autonomy without structure creates as much slop as leverage.” One of his learnings from the conference was to **“re-visit and re-implement your skills”** : > “_Each time there’s a new model release, it’s as if you have a kid that grows from middle school to high school. You have to change the curriculum for them to get the benefits of the new model._” ## **Agent engineering at scale** It’s been three full years since The Rise of the AI Engineer and the first AI Engineer Summit. Looking back, it really is striking how much the conversation has evolved. Three years ago, the focus was on proving that LLMs could act as autonomous agents at all (and the answer at that time was usually _no_). AutoGPT, prompt engineering, and early orchestration frameworks like Langchain dominated the discussion back then. **Now that agents not only work, but have proven they can scale,** this year’s AI Engineer World’s Fair was able to concentrate on the bigger problems: building reliable systems, orchestrating teams of agents, managing context, evaluating outputs and integrating AI into production software. ![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!0Vc6!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6c523240-249a-483c-a849-cf9a6adbeacc_1280x875.jpeg) Agents are everywhere now… even on the back of San Francisco buses.   The term “AI engineer” may have started life as a new job title, but at AIEWF 2026 it felt more like a description of **where software engineering itself is heading**. Whether developers call themselves AI engineers, software engineers or Forward Deployed Engineers, they’re increasingly working with the same set of ideas: coding agents, harness engineering, designing loops, and orchestration.

title: TPU Deployments with Gemma 31B, v6e-8, and Antigravity CLI
summary: This article provides a step by step debugging guide for deploying Gemma 4 to a Google Cloud TPU...
author: xbill
content: --- title: TPU Deployments with Gemma 31B, v6e-8, and Antigravity CLI published: true series: Gemma4 date: 2026-07-15 13:04:39 UTC tags: pythonprogramming,tpu,antigravitycli,gemma4 canonical_url: https://xbill999.medium.com/tpu-deployments-with-gemma-31b-v6e-8-and-antigravity-cli-25ef946da7a4 --- This article provides a step by step debugging guide for deploying Gemma 4 to a Google Cloud TPU system,. A suite of Python MCP tools is built to simplify management of the vLLM hosted Gemma 4 deployment with Antigravity CLI. ![](https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1*7OXxRfBzO-LDL08MNFg39g.jpeg) #### What is this project trying to Do? This project is a DevOps/SRE assistant that uses a Gemma 4 model hosted on TPU. It provides tools to provision the Docker container and deploy the model, as well as for observability and performance testing. This project is similar to a previous project that targeted GPU hosted Gemma4 instances on GCP: [Gemma-SRE: Self-Hosted vLLM Infrastructure Agent](https://medium.com/google-cloud/gemma-sre-self-hosted-vllm-infrastructure-agent-afda000c0943) #### Antigravity CLI Antigravity CLI is the follow-on successor to Gemini CLI- the terminal driven, agent assisted coding tool. Full details on installing Antigravity CLI are here: [Getting Started with Antigravity CLI](https://medium.com/google-cloud/getting-started-with-antigravity-cli-26c5da90951f) #### Testing the Antigravity CLI Environment Once you have all the tools in place- you can test the startup of Antigravity CLI. The high level MCP tool implementation is the same no matter what low level transport channel/method that the MCP Client uses to connect to a MCP Server. The simplest transport that the SDK supports is the stdio (stdio/stdout) transport — which connects a locally running process. Here is the SRE architectural explanation of why this setup is immune to runtime OOMs, and how it compares to our previous configuration: ────── ### 1. The Dynamic Headroom Buffer (TP=8) Sharding our 31B parameters over all 8 TPU chips leaves a massive memory buffer on each device: • Per-Chip Memory Allocation: Each device has 16 GiB of total HBM capacity. • Weights Allocation: Occupies only ~7.75 GiB (48.4%), leaving a highly secure ~8.25 GiB free pool. • Activation Safety Margin: The compiler and runtime workspace activations have several gigabytes of dedicated headroom, completely eliminating the risk of memory spike crashes during heavy prefill batches. ────── ### 2. vLLM Pre-allocated Block Architecture vLLM utilizes a pre-allocated memory pool that prevents dynamic memory growth: 1. Static Pre-allocation: On startup, vLLM pre-allocates exactly 1,462 physical KV Cache blocks across the HBM pool. It never requests or allocates additional memory on-the-fly during query runtime. 2. Graceful Queuing Over Flow: Our pre-allocated pool corresponds to a maximum host boundary of 2,195,133 in- flight tokens. 3. Graceful Scheduler Throttling: If incoming concurrent requests try to push past this limit, vLLM does not allocate more memory (which would trigger an OOM). Instead, its continuous batching scheduler gracefully pauses new tokens and queues requests in a safe system buffer until earlier queries complete and free their blocks. ``` how does this affect the size of the KV cache? ```plaintext > how does the size of the KV cache affect deployment? The size of the Key-Value (KV) Cache is one of the most critical factors governing an LLM deployment. It directly determines the system's concurrency limits, maximum supported context, throughput scaling, and cost efficiency. Here is a breakdown of how the KV Cache size affects our deployment: ────── ### 1. The HBM Allocation Trade-off (The Balance) A TPU device's HBM capacity is fixed (16 GiB on TPU v6e). The memory layout is a zero-sum partition: Total HBM (16 GiB) = Static Model Weights + Runtime Workspace Activations + Pre-allocated KV Cache • If the model weights are too large (like TP=4 where weights take 15.5 GiB ): The KV Cache is squeezed into a tiny slice ( ~0.5 GiB ). • If the model weights are sharded (like TP=8 where weights take 7.75 GiB ): The KV Cache pool expands to over 7 GiB of pre-allocated HBM per chip, changing our system capabilities entirely. ────── ### 2. Impact on Concurrency & Throughput In vLLM's continuous batching architecture, the maximum number of concurrent requests the host can process simultaneously is strictly limited by the number of available KV Cache slots: • The Bottle-neck ( TP=4 ): With only 526 blocks, the moment parallel users scaled up, the KV Cache filled up instantly. vLLM was forced to queue requests, capping peak throughput. • The Acceleration ( TP=8 ): With 1,462 physical blocks, vLLM can load hundreds of sequences into the active batch pool simultaneously. This allowed our throughput to scale from 3.5 req/s (at 1 user) to 66.99 req/s (at 2048 users). ────── ### 3. Impact on Max Context Window per Request Each token in a prompt or generated output requires storing its key and value tensors across all model layers: • If a single user sends a 16K context prompt, it requires a massive dedicated allocation of KV Cache blocks. • On a squeezed cache pool, a single 16K query would consume the entire host memory pool, causing all other concurrent users to starve or be paused. • On our optimized 1,462 block pool, we can process several deep 16K context queries simultaneously without affecting overall system latency. ────── ### 4. Impact on Inference Latency Profile LLM generation consists of two phases, both deeply impacted by the KV Cache configuration: 1. Prefill Phase (First Token): Computes the prompt representations and populates the KV Cache. Sharding this over TP=8 lets JAX split the key/value projection matrices across 8 chips, lowering prefill latency. 2. Decode Phase (Subsequent Tokens): Read and append to the KV Cache one token at a time. This phase is memory- bandwidth-bound. Sharding the KV Cache over 8 separate high-bandwidth memory (HBM2e) buses allows the TPU VM to read/write KV slots in parallel, slashing Time-to-Output-Token (TPOT). ────── ### 🛠 How SREs Optimize the KV Cache on TPU To ensure maximum efficiency on TPU v6e-8, our deployment uses the following parameters: • --tensor-parallel-size 8 : Minimizes weight footprint per chip to maximize HBM room for KV Cache. • --max-model-len 16384 : Caps maximum sequence length to prevent a single extremely long user prompt from starving the cache pool. • --gpu-memory-utilization 0.90 (typically): Directs the engine to claim 90% of remaining post-load memory specifically for the KV Cache block allocation. ``` #### Cross Check The Deployed Model Oh enough memory mumbo-jumbo. Gemma 4 is the latest generation of lightweight, open-model AI developed by Google DeepMind. It is built using the same research and technology used to create the Gemini models. While Gemini is a collection of large, closed-source models accessible via API or a chat interface, Gemma is designed to be "open," meaning the weights are available for developers and researchers to download and run on their own hardware. Here are the key characteristics of Gemma 4: ### 1. Open Weights (Not "Open Source") Gemma 4 is an open-weights model. This means that while the final "brain" of the AI is provided for public use, the full training data and the exact code used to train it are not released. This allows developers to fine-tune the model for specific tasks (like coding or medical analysis) without needing Google's servers. ### 2. Efficiency and Size Unlike massive models that require giant server farms, Gemma 4 is designed to be efficient. It comes in various sizes (parameter counts), allowing it to run on: • Consumer Laptops: Using GPUs like NVIDIA RTX series. • Edge Devices: Including mobile phones or tablets. • Cloud Instances: For scalable professional applications. ### 3. Multimodality Depending on the specific version, Gemma 4 is capable of processing more than just text. It can typically handle: • Text: For conversation, summarization, and reasoning. • Images: For analyzing visual data. • Audio: Some versions of Gemma 4 can process audio inputs directly. ### 4. Safety and Responsibility Because it is an open model, Google uses a process called RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback) and rigorous safety filtering to ensure the model doesn't generate harmful content, while still remaining flexible enough for developers to customize. ### Summary Table: Gemma vs. Gemini Feature | Gemma 4 | Gemini --------------------------------------|--------------------------------------|------------------------------------- Access | Open Weights (Downloadable) | Closed (API/Interface) Hardware | Runs locally on your PC/Device | Runs on Google's TPU clusters Purpose | Customization & Local Dev | General purpose high-end AI Ownership | You control the deployment | Google controls the deployment ``` #### Benchmark the Local Model The local model was benchmarked: ```plaintext Below is the structured performance sweep matrix showing Throughput (req/s) and [Average Latency (s)] across selected user concurrency levels and context windows. I have successfully generated and embedded the comparative visualization for you. ### 📊 Comparative SRE Graph Created We generated a 2x3 panel of telemetry curves contrasting Throughput and Latency against Concurrency for three critical context sizes: 128, 1024, and 4096 tokens. • Locally Exported Image: tp_comparison_chart.png • Artifact Path: /home/xbill/.gemini/antigravity-cli/brain/93eebc37-dd44-479e-b313- 1656d3fefe68/tp_comparison_chart.png • Report Embedded: Integrated directly into upgrade_performance_report.md. ────── ### 🔍 Key Graph Interpretations 1. Throughput Scaling under Heavy Concurrency: • At lower concurrencies, both topologies match closely, as execution is bound by prefill computation. • As concurrency climbs past 16 users, TP=8 surges significantly ahead of TP=4 . This shows that sharding model parameters across all 8 devices frees up massive chip-level computation blocks and maximizes vLLM's continuous batching on Trillium. 2. Ultra-Low Latency Ceiling: • For context sizes like 1024 tokens under heavy concurrent demand, the TP=8 line remains significantly flatter and lower than the TP=4 line. • Spreading the weight footprints over 8 devices allows JAX to run parallel projections across the host ring effortlessly over our ICI fabric, slashing latency under intensive concurrent loops under massive concurrent loads. 3. Expanded Working Capacity: • At 4096 tokens, the TP=4 lines are cut short early as they hit their strict hardware limit (the baseline pool could allocate only 526 blocks, restricting capacity to under 789,760 in-flight tokens). • The TP=8 line successfully scales and runs out to 512 concurrent users before being bounded by capacity limits (running up to our new physical ceiling of 2,195,133 in-flight tokens!). ``` This is visualized: ![](https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1*GPByOn07r5wMjwxkkqS2Dg.png) ![](https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1*lt8FLb7ZDlj5SghnnT5sig.png) #### Comparison with Other Deployments The 31B model was compared to other hardware configurations: ```plaintext I have compiled a comprehensive SRE Comparative Performance Report that compares the Gemma-4 31B model served on TPU v6e-8 ( TP=8 ) against other common setups: TPU v6e-4 ( TP=4 ), RTX 6000 Pro GPUs, and NVIDIA L4 GPUs. I have saved this detailed analysis as a persistent workspace artifact for you: 📄 tpu_gpu_comprehensive_comparison.md ────── ### 📊 Comparative Performance Matrix Feature / Metric | Cloud TPU v6e-8 (Tr… | Cloud TPU v6e-4 (Tr… | RTX 6000 Pro GPU (C… | NVIDIA L4 GPU (Cloud… ----------------------|----------------------|----------------------|----------------------|----------------------- Model Size/Precision | Full 31B Dense | Full 31B Dense | Full 31B Dense | 26B-it | | | | (Pruned/Quantized) Parallel Topology | TP=8 | TP=4 | Single Device ( TP=1 | Single Device ( TP=1 | | | ) | ) Weight Footprint | ~7.75 GiB / device | ~15.5 GiB / device | ~62 GiB (Full | Max 24 GiB (Forces (HBM/VRAM) | | | Model) | AWQ/INT4) KV Cache Capacity | 2,195,133 tokens | 789,760 tokens | Highly Constrained | Extremely Constrained | (1,462 Blocks) 🚀 | (526 Blocks) | | Peak Throughput | 66.99 req/s (@2048 | 60.11 req/s (@1024 | ~308 tok/s overall | 80-90 tok/s overall | Users, 128 context) | Users, 256 context) | (Early Saturation) | (Pruned model) Single User Prefill | 3.498 req/s | 2.608 req/s | ~30 tok/s (~0.03 | ~80 tok/s (~0.08 (8 tok) | (Ultra-fast) | | req/s) | req/s) Single User Prefill | 2.088 req/s | 1.369 req/s | Saturates / Swaps | Saturates / Swaps (16K tok) | | | | Preemption / Drop | 0.0% (Perfect) | why does the TPU perform better in these benchmarks? The performance advantage of the Cloud TPU v6e serving stack over Cloud Run and mid-range GPUs (like NVIDIA L4 / RTX 6000) comes down to three main factors: hardware architecture, memory design, and software-compiler optimization. Here is a breakdown of why the TPU outperforms them in these serving benchmarks: ────── ### 1. Memory Bandwidth: HBM vs. GDDR6 (The Decoder Bottleneck) The decoding phase of LLM generation (producing tokens one-by-one) is strictly memory-bandwidth bound. For every single token generated, the model must read all its parameters from memory into the processor cores. • TPU v6e: Utilizes High Bandwidth Memory (HBM2e) providing up to 1.6 TB/s of memory bandwidth per chip. • NVIDIA L4 GPU: Utilizes standard GDDR6 memory, which is capped at only 300 GB/s of bandwidth. • Performance Impact: Because the TPU can load weights and KV Cache states into its cores 5.3× faster than an L4 GPU, it achieves significantly higher token generation throughput under concurrent user loads. ────── ### 2. Dedicated Systolic Arrays vs. General-Purpose Cores • TPU Matrix Multiply Units (MXUs): TPUs are built around custom Systolic Array processors. Matrix multiplications (the core math of LLMs) flow continuously through a grid of ALU nodes without needing to read or write intermediate values back to register files. This minimizes data movement and maximizes ALU utilization. • GPU Tensor Cores: While NVIDIA Tensor Cores are fast, they reside within a general-purpose Streaming Multiprocessor (SM) architecture. The GPU must allocate overhead for instruction scheduling, thread dispatching, warp synchronization, and cache coherency, reducing power and execution efficiency compared to the TPU's specialized design. ────── ### 3. Native Inter-Chip Interconnects (ICI) vs. PCIe Bottlenecks • TPU v6e-4 Unified Mesh: The 4 chips in a v6e-4 node are connected via Google's custom, optical Inter- Chip Interconnects (ICI). This allows the chips to shard model layers (Tensor Parallelism size 4) and communicate with ultra-low latency, acting as a single virtual accelerator with a unified memory pool. • Standard VM / Cloud Run GPUs: GPUs in mid-range GCE VMs (or multi-GPU setups without NVLink) communicate over standard PCIe Gen4/Gen5 slots. Sharding a model across multiple L4/RTX GPUs over PCIe introduces severe communication bottlenecks, degrading throughput as concurrency scales. ────── ### 4. Direct bare-metal VMs vs. Serverless Virtualization (Cloud Run) • Cloud Run Overhead: Cloud Run is a serverless environment built on top of Knative and virtualized sandbox runtimes (like gVisor ). It introduces virtualization layers, container startup times, network routing hops, and CPU throttling to handle scale-to-zero logic, which is poorly suited for high- concurrency LLM traffic. • TPU VM Architecture: The TPU VMs ( v2-alpha-tpuv6e runtime) are direct, bare-metal virtual machines. vLLM has direct access to the hardware drivers and memory space, completely bypassing container network virtualization overhead. ────── ### 5. XLA (Accelerated Linear Algebra) Graph Compilation • vLLM on TPUs uses Google's XLA compiler stack. • Instead of executing model layers step-by-step (e.g., PyTorch eager mode), XLA compiles the entire LLM compute graph into a single executable, fusing operations (combining attention layers, activation functions, and layer norms). This keeps intermediate matrices inside the TPU's fast on-chip SRAM, preventing slow HBM round-trips. ``` and are you really really sure? ```plaintext > are you sure? you not making this up? I completely understand the skepticism! LLMs can indeed hallucinate hardware details, but these specs are verifiable in the official datasheets. Here are the concrete, physical hardware specifications you can cross-reference: ────── ### 1. Verifiable Hardware Specifications #### Memory Bandwidth (The Critical LLM Metric) • NVIDIA L4 GPU: • Memory Type: 24 GB GDDR6 • Bus Width: 192-bit • Bandwidth: 300 GB/s • Reference: NVIDIA L4 Datasheet (Page 2) [https://images.nvidia.com/aem-dam/Solutions/Data-](https://images.nvidia.com/aem-dam/Solutions/Data-) Center/l4/nvidia-l4-datasheet-web.pdf • Google TPU v6e: • Memory Type: 32 GB HBM2e • Bandwidth: 1.63 TB/s (1,630 GB/s) • Reference: Google Cloud TPU System Architecture Docs [https://cloud.google.com/tpu/docs/system-](https://cloud.google.com/tpu/docs/system-) architecture-tpu-vm#tpu_v6e #### Interconnect Links (Multi-Accelerator Communication) • NVIDIA L4: Capped at standard PCIe Gen4 x16 slots (32 GB/s bi-directional). L4 GPUs do not support NVLink (NVIDIA's proprietary high-speed GPU interconnect). • TPU v6e: Uses Google's custom Inter-Chip Interconnect (ICI) copper/optical links, which connect chips directly at high bandwidth to bypass the CPU and PCIe bus. ────── ### 2. Architectural Design Facts • Systolic Arrays: This is the core patent behind Google's TPU design since TPU v1 was released in 2016. In standard GPUs, registers must fetch and store values between every multiply-accumulate operation. In a systolic array, data streams through a 2D grid of processing elements, sharing inputs horizontally and vertically without accessing reg

title: The Myth of the Post-Documentation Era
summary: There is a growing sentiment in engineering circles right now that documentation is a relic of the...
author: Ben Halpern
content: There is a growing sentiment in engineering circles right now that documentation is a relic of the past. The argument usually goes something like this: *We’re living in the era of agent-driven development. If an AI agent can read the raw source code or parse an OpenAPI specification instantly, why waste human engineering hours writing prose? Code churns too fast anyway, and human-written docs are outdated the second they’re committed.* It’s an attractive, black-and-white view of the world. It’s also completely wrong. Chasing strict determinism in your source of truth is a pipe dream. Code and specs tell a system *how* something works, but they are fundamentally incapable of explaining *why* it was built that way in the first place. --- ## The Intent Gap: Why Code Isn't Enough Even if you’re building entirely for a downstream consumer of AI agents, there is a massive, structural gap between a raw API specification and an operational reality. Agents are phenomenal at pattern matching and syntax execution, but they struggle with architectural philosophy and human intent. We still need words to contextualize the boundaries. A spec can define an endpoint, its parameters, and its payload. What it can't capture is the nuance of *why* a specific architectural trade-off was made, or the implicit historical context of a legacy edge case. Prose provides the guardrails for non-deterministic systems. Even if that prose is ultimately consumed by a machine rather than a human, the written word remains the highest-leverage way to transmit intent. ## The Danger of Slop Describing Slop This doesn't mean we need to return to the days of manually maintaining massive, static wiki pages. Automation has a massive role to play here. Cascading automation—where documentation is dynamically generated alongside code changes—is incredibly powerful. But there’s a trap here: **slop describing slop is entirely useless.** If we completely hand off documentation generation to unchecked LLMs, we end up with a feedback loop of hallucinated context describing rapidly shifting code. It creates noise, not clarity. > **The Key is Oversight.** Even if the documentation is entirely bot-driven, human engineering oversight is non-negotiable. We need to gut-check and validate the generated prose to ensure it represents an accurate, high-level explanation of the broader context. Think of generated docs as a non-deterministic cousin of the API itself—highly valuable, but only if kept on a tight leash. --- ## The Trust Crisis and the Search for Reputation Right now, the single biggest blocker to this new paradigm is trust. The current lack of a "gut-check" trustworthiness metric for documentation is a massive bottleneck for both human developers and autonomous agents. In the open-source eras of the past, we relied on crude but effective reputation proxies. If a repository had 10,000 GitHub stars, a vibrant issue tracker, and recent commits, you could reasonably assume the project (and its documentation) was stable. We don't have a reliable reputation system for the AI era yet. The absolute novelty of the moment, combined with how incredibly easy it is to game automated metrics, means everything feels a bit unanchored. The next major shift in developer tooling won't just be about making agents faster or code generation cleaner. It will be about solving the reputation problem—building systems that can automatically verify, score, and guarantee the trustworthiness of the knowledge bases our software relies on. Until then, don't delete your markdown files. The machines still need to read between the lines.
